title: Design a File Storage System (like Google Drive/S3) — chunked uploads, deduplication, metadata database, access control, versioning, CDN for downloads.
shortTitle: Design a File Storage System (like Google Drive/S3)

s1_definition.profdef: A file storage system stores and serves large binary objects reliably and at scale by splitting files into fixed-size chunks for resumable uploads, deduplicating identical chunks by content hash to save space, recording file and chunk metadata in a database separate from the blob store, enforcing access control, maintaining version history, and serving downloads through a content delivery network. The object data lives in a blob store while the metadata layer coordinates everything.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must store millions of scanned loan documents and statements for Rajesh and Priya. Instead of keeping one giant file, the bank cuts each document into small pieces, notices when two documents share identical pieces and stores that piece only once, keeps an index card describing which pieces make up which document and who may see it, keeps older versions in case a page is replaced, and serves popular documents from nearby copies so downloads are fast. That filing system is exactly what S3 or Google Drive does at massive scale.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split files into chunks for resumable uploads, dedupe chunks by hash, keep metadata separate from blobs, enforce access control, version files, and serve downloads via CDN.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A file storage system stores and serves large binary objects reliably and at scale by splitting files into fixed-size chunks for resumable uploads, deduplicating identical chunks by content hash to save space, recording file and chunk metadata in a database separate from the blob store, enforcing access control, maintaining version history, and serving downloads through a content delivery network. The object data lives in a blob store while the metadata layer coordinates everything.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must store millions of scanned loan documents and statements for Rajesh and Priya. Instead of keeping one giant file, the bank cuts each document into small pieces, notices when two documents share identical pieces and stores that piece only once, keeps an index card describing which pieces make up which document and who may see it, keeps older versions in case a page is replaced, and serves popular documents from nearby copies so downloads are fast. That filing system is exactly what S3 or Google Drive does at massive scale.

**One line to remember:** Split files into chunks for resumable uploads, dedupe chunks by hash, keep metadata separate from blobs, enforce access control, version files, and serve downloads via CDN.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh uploads a large scanned loan agreement over a shaky mobile connection, and if the upload fails at ninety percent, forcing him to restart from zero is a terrible experience. The real problem is resumable, reliable upload of big files. This is exactly how chunked upload by content hash works.

Problem 2 — thousands of customers upload the same standard terms-and-conditions PDF as part of their application, and storing millions of identical copies wastes huge amounts of storage. This is exactly how content-hash deduplication saves space.

Problem 3 — a loan document is strictly confidential, so only Rajesh and his assigned officer may read it, and when a corrected page replaces an old one, the bank must keep the prior version for audit. These are exactly the access-control and versioning features.

We build a runnable storage core: a `Chunker`, a `BlobStore` keyed by content hash with dedup, a `MetadataStore` for file records with versions and permissions, and a `FileStorageService` for upload, download with access control, and version listing. The demo uploads Rajesh's loan document, uploads an identical shared PDF to show dedup, enforces access control against Priya, and creates a new version.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

# Run the storage demo
java -cp target/file-storage-1.0.0.jar com.bank.storage.StorageDemo
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is Rajesh's loan document, the same standard terms PDF uploaded by both Rajesh and Priya, an unauthorized download attempt by Priya, an authorized one by Rajesh, and a replacement version.

Step 1: The loan document enters `upload`. The chunker splits it into four-kilobyte pieces and hashes each. Each unique chunk is stored once in the blob store, and the ordered list of chunk hashes plus owner and readers is saved as version one metadata.

Step 2: The identical terms PDF is uploaded twice under two different file ids. The first upload stores its chunks; the second finds every chunk hash already present and stores nothing new, so the unique chunk count does not grow for the second upload. This is deduplication.

Step 3: Priya attempts to download the loan document. The metadata says only Rajesh and the officer may read it, so `canRead` returns false and a SecurityException is thrown, logged as an expected access denial.

Step 4: Rajesh downloads version one; the service reassembles the chunks in order into the original bytes. Then a corrected document is uploaded as version two, which creates a new metadata record while version one's chunks remain, so both versions are listed. The data that changed is the blob store growing only by truly new chunks and the metadata gaining a new version.

```
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] stored loan-SAV2001 v1 with N chunks
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] stored terms-A v1 with M chunks
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] stored terms-B v1 with M chunks
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] Total unique chunks stored: (no growth from terms-B)
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [WARNING] Access denied as expected: CUR3001 may not read loan-SAV2001
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] Rajesh downloaded 3500 bytes (v1)
2026-10-31 23:20:00 [INFO] Versions of loan doc: [1, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  upload loan doc (owner SAV2001, readers {SAV2001, OFFICER-9})
    │ Chunker.split → [c1,c2,c3...]
    │ hash each chunk
    ▼
  BlobStore.putIfAbsent(hash, bytes)
    │
    ├─ hash new → store                ├─ hash exists → DEDUP (skip)
    ▼                                  ▼
  MetadataStore.save(v1, [hashes], readers)

  download(loan, v1, user)
    │ MetadataStore.get
    │
    ├─ user is reader?                 ├─ user NOT reader
    │  YES → reassemble chunks         │  NO → SecurityException
    ▼                                  ▼
  file bytes                         403 denied

  upload v2 → new metadata record, old chunks retained → versions [1,2]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — File Storage Service ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Content-addressed storage: key = SHA-256 → auto dedup    │
  │  Metadata/blob separation: DB coordinates, blobs scale    │
  │  Versioning: immutable metadata records per version       │
  │  Guard clause ACL: canRead before reassembly              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Chunker splits, BlobStore stores, MetadataStore indexes│
  │  O: add encryption-at-rest = wrap BlobStore, no edits     │
  │  D: Service depends on store abstractions                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ FileStorageService   │─────▶│       Chunker        │
  │ - chunker,blobs,meta │ uses │ + split/hash         │
  │ + upload/download    │      └──────────────────────┘
  │ + versions           │      ┌──────────────────────┐
  └──────────┬───────────┘─────▶│      BlobStore       │
             │ uses             │ + putIfAbsent/get    │
             ▼                  └──────────────────────┘
      ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
      │ MetadataStore│          │    FileMetadata      │
      │ + save/get   │─creates─▶│ - version, chunkHashes│
      │ + versions   │          │ + canRead(user)      │
      └──────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: File version ────────────────────────────

  [UPLOADING] ──chunks stored──→ [v1 COMMITTED] ──new upload──→ [v2 COMMITTED]
                                      │
                                      │ v1 chunks still referenced
                                      ▼
                                 [RESTORABLE]

  ── Call Chain (upload) ────────────────────────────────────

  1. service.upload(fileId, owner, bytes, readers)
  2.   → chunker.split(bytes) → chunks
  3.   → for each: hash → blobs.putIfAbsent (dedup)
  4.   → meta.nextVersion(fileId)
  5.   → meta.save(metadata)

  Contract for download(fileId, version, user):
    Pre:  file/version exists
    Post: returns bytes only if user canRead; else SecurityException
    Reassembles chunks in recorded order
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A file storage system stores and serves large binary objects reliably and at scale, and I build it around a clean separation between the blob store that holds raw bytes and the metadata layer that coordinates everything. The first technique is chunked upload: I split a large file into fixed-size pieces, each identified by the hash of its content, and upload them independently. This makes uploads resumable, so if the network drops after seven of ten chunks, the client resends only the missing three rather than the entire file, which is a huge win on mobile connections.

The second technique is deduplication by content hash. Before storing a chunk I check whether a chunk with that hash already exists, and if so I just reference it instead of storing a duplicate. Because two identical documents or two copies of the same attachment produce identical chunk hashes, this saves enormous space. In the National Bank of India context, thousands of loan applications include the same standard terms-and-conditions PDF, and deduplication means the bank stores those identical chunks once rather than millions of times.

The metadata database is deliberately separate from the blob store. The blob store holds chunk bytes keyed by hash and scales for raw throughput, while the metadata database records which chunks in which order form each file, along with owner, size, timestamps, version, and permissions, and stays relationally queryable. Access control is checked on every read and write so only the owner or allowed readers can fetch a confidential loan document, and versioning stores a new immutable metadata record per change while old chunks remain referenced, so a previous version can be restored for audit.

The senior details I emphasize are the delivery and security paths. Uploads go directly to the blob store through pre-signed URLs so file bytes never pass through the application servers and overload them, and downloads of popular files are served through a content delivery network with signed, time-limited URLs so the origin is protected and only authorized users can fetch. That combination of chunked resumable uploads, content-hash deduplication, separated metadata, strict access control, versioning, and CDN delivery is what lets a file storage system be simultaneously space-efficient, reliable, secure, and fast.
